positions.position: Remove 'The filter does not understand the message; it only counts clues' from the explain stage to keep the pace up; learners saw it in the compare block.
Blocking ai-framing flag: without the line, the explanation leaves learners believing the filter understands messages.

resolutions.resolution: Keep the line in the explain stage. The designer may tighten the wording or merge it into an existing sentence so it reads briskly, provided the meaning (no understanding, only counting clues) stays explicit.
resolutions.reason: Accuracy outranks experience. The flag is upheld, not overruled. The designer's goal of pace is served by tightening the line rather than removing it.

positions.position: Use a cricket chase (150 runs is the line) in the base English analogy for threshold; it is vivid for Indian learners.
Cricket is culture-specific; the base analogy must use a universal source, with cricket only in the hi and te locale variants.

resolutions.resolution: Base English analogy uses a universal source with the same structure (for example, collecting marks across an exam until you reach the pass mark, every mark adds up, the pass mark is the line), with its break point stated. The cricket chase goes into the hi and te locale variants, also with its break point stated.
resolutions.reason: Clarity (Article 7: source domains recognisable anywhere; culture-specific examples only in locale variants) outranks experience, and both positions can be kept: universal base, cricket in locale variants where it is vivid.

positions.position: Make the hook a 120-word atmospheric story about a late-night scam message to build tension.
Rohit (class 10, Hindi, shared phone) lost the thread in the long hook; keep it under 40 words.

resolutions.resolution: Hook stays under 40 words. The designer keeps the late-night scam-message tension in that space (for example, one message shown on screen at 11:47 pm with a single question that asks the learner to decide: junk or real?).
resolutions.reason: Clarity outranks experience; a novice learner losing the thread on screen one is a clarity failure. The designer's goal of tension is served within the word limit.

positions.position: The core path cannot fit 20 minutes without dropping break-it, which the lesson grammar requires; it needs about 30 minutes.
Cut break-it to meet the 20-minute target.

resolutions.resolution: Cutting break-it is rejected: clarity outranks experience and Article 5 requires the stage. But keeping the full arc contradicts the creator's stated '20 minutes, it is a taster', so the creator decides the length. Draft is held at the full arc pending decision.
resolutions.reason: The priority order settles the narrow question (break-it stays), but the result conflicts with the creator's stated intent, which must be escalated.
options: Accept a ~30-minute core path with the full arc.
Keep 20 minutes: compress break-it to one short act and move other depth into optional detours (curriculum designer to confirm it fits).
Split into two linked ~15-minute parts, with break-it opening part two.

positions.position: Build a new 'race' component where two filters compete on a message stream, showing speed and accuracy together.
Use the existing compare component; a new component is not needed for the objective.

resolutions.resolution: The draft uses the existing compare component now, so the lesson is not blocked. Whether to commission a new 'race' component is the creator's decision, because new components are on the always-ask list.
resolutions.reason: Building a new component is an always-ask action; I cannot approve it. The objective is met by the existing component, so the draft does not wait on the decision.
options: Keep the compare component; no new component.
Commission the 'race' component as a versioned plugin for later use, and keep compare in this lesson.
Commission it and swap it into this lesson once built and reviewed.

positions.position: Blocking sourcing flag: 'hundreds of clues' is a specific unsourced claim.
It is a fair simplification and the number makes the contrast with three clues vivid; keep it.

resolutions.resolution: Remove the unsourced number. Rewrite to 'Real filters use far more clues than our three, and many learn which clues matter from examples.' If a citable source for a specific figure is found, the number may return with the citation after the reviewer clears it.
resolutions.reason: Accuracy outranks clarity, and the flag is resolved by a change that removes the problem, not by overruling it. The contrast with three clues stays vivid without the unsourced figure.

positions.position: Warm amber chapter colour for 'transfer-reflect'; it feels reflective.
Cool violet; amber already carries meaning elsewhere. Both pass all contrast and accessibility checks; the disagreement is purely visual.

resolutions.resolution: Creator chooses the chapter colour. Draft uses a placeholder token until decided.
resolutions.reason: Both positions serve the same priority (aesthetics) and cannot both be kept, so the order does not settle it.

positions.position: Ask learners to paste real messages from their own inbox for authenticity.
Blocking privacy flag: real messages contain names, numbers and other people's personal data; use made-up messages.

resolutions.resolution: Learners use made-up messages only; no real inbox content is requested or entered. For authenticity, provide a realistic, invented message set (delivery scams, bank alerts, school notices) and let learners write their own fictional junk message to test.
resolutions.reason: Safety outranks experience, and Article 10 forbids collecting children's personal data. The flag is upheld; the designer's authenticity goal is served with realistic invented messages.

positions.position: Use the creator's opening line 'AI thinks like a brain, so how does it decide what is junk?' as written.
Blocking ai-framing flag: 'AI thinks like a brain' gives the filter a mind, and the lesson never shows the break point.

resolutions.resolution: The line is not used as written in the draft until the creator decides. Creator chooses how to resolve the clash between the requested opening and the accuracy flag.
resolutions.reason: Using the line would override an accuracy flag; changing it contradicts the creator's stated intent. Both conditions require escalation.
options: Reword the opening, e.g. 'Your phone hides some messages as junk. How does it decide?'
Keep the line but add an explicit break-point moment where learners see the filter only counts clues and does not think (satisfies Article 7).
Recast it as a question to test: 'Does AI think like a brain? Let's see how it decides what is junk.'

positions.position: Publish now so schools can use it before term starts next week.
Hindi and Telugu are drafts until native speakers review them; publish English only, and only when the creator decides.

resolutions.resolution: Nothing is published by me. Publishing is an always-ask action; the creator decides. Hindi and Telugu remain drafts until native-speaker review regardless.
resolutions.reason: Publishing is on the always-ask list. Accuracy (unreviewed translations, Article 11) outranks experience, so publishing hi and te now is not offered.
options: Publish English only now; hi and te after native-speaker review.
Wait and publish all three locales together after review.
Hold publication until the open decisions above are settled.

creatorSummary.made: A validated draft of the junk-filter lesson (English base, Hindi and Telugu translation drafts). Nothing published.
creatorSummary.flagsAndResolutions: Resolved by priority order: kept the 'does not understand, only counts clues' line (accuracy over pace); universal base analogy for threshold with cricket in hi/te variants; hook cut to under 40 words with tension kept; 'hundreds of clues' replaced with wording that makes no unsourced claim; real inbox messages replaced by invented ones (privacy). No safety or accuracy flag was overruled.
forYourDecision: c4 Length: accept ~30 min, compress break-it into 20 min, or split into two parts (break-it stays in all options).
c5 New 'race' component: none, build for later, or build and swap in (draft uses compare meanwhile).
c7 Chapter colour: amber or violet (both pass accessibility).
c9 Your opening line 'AI thinks like a brain' conflicts with an accuracy flag: reword, keep with an explicit break-point moment, or recast as a question to test.
c10 Publishing: English only now, all locales after review, or hold.
weaknesses: Lesson currently runs about 30 minutes, over your 20-minute target.
Hindi and Telugu are unreviewed by native speakers.
Opening line and chapter colour are placeholders until you decide.
Replacement analogy and the reworded clue sentence have not yet been tested with the novice panel.
